questions.q: Under PostgreSQL's MVCC model, what actually happens when a row is UPDATEd?
options: A new row version is written and the old version is marked no-longer-current, rather than overwriting the row in place
The row is immediately overwritten in place with no history kept
The row is deleted and re-inserted with a new primary key
The change is written only to the WAL and never to the table
questions.explain: MVCC keeps the old version around (as a dead tuple once no transaction needs it) so concurrent readers can still see a consistent snapshot.

options: A row version no active transaction can see anymore, but which still physically occupies space
A row that has been permanently deleted from disk
A corrupted row that failed a checksum
A row waiting to be indexed
questions.explain: Dead tuples are the leftover old row versions from UPDATEs and DELETEs under MVCC — no longer visible, but not yet reclaimed.

questions.q: What is the key difference between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL?
options: VACUUM marks dead tuple space reusable without shrinking the file; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and returns space to the OS but requires an exclusive lock
VACUUM and VACUUM FULL do exactly the same thing
VACUUM FULL runs automatically every night while VACUUM must be run manually
VACUUM only works on indexes, VACUUM FULL only works on tables
questions.explain: Plain VACUUM reclaims space for reuse within the existing file; VACUUM FULL is a heavier, lock-exclusive rewrite that actually shrinks the file on disk.

questions.q: What is table bloat, per this lesson?
options: Dead tuples accumulating faster than vacuuming reclaims them, growing the table beyond what live data needs
A table that has too many indexes
A table that exceeds PostgreSQL's maximum row limit
A normal, harmless side effect of running ANALYZE
questions.explain: When vacuuming — manual or auto — falls behind the rate of dead tuple creation, the table and its indexes grow larger than the live data requires.

questions.q: What can cause autovacuum to fall behind on a table, per this lesson?
options: A long-running transaction holding back what VACUUM can consider dead, or autovacuum settings too conservative for the table's write volume
Running too many SELECT queries against the table
Having too few columns in the table
Using a B-tree index instead of a GIN index
questions.explain: MVCC must preserve row versions a still-running transaction might need to see, and conservative autovacuum thresholds can let dead tuples pile up on high-write tables.
